Q: html5 canvas always returns 8bits of color when using getImageData() A:

It's 2026, and it's now possible to do this.

You can now set a colorType for a 2D canvas when creating the context, as described in the spec, and on MDN:

This can be applied like so, canvas.getContext('2d', { colorType: 'float16' });

You can then get data in RGBA16 from the canvas using

const float16ImageData = context.getImageData(0, 0, 1, 1, {
  pixelFormat: "rgba-float16",
});

Please remember that the above will return a Float16Array and not Uint8ClampedArray . The values range between [0, 1].

If you need to read 16 bit data from an image, e.g. height maps, then this can prove to be quite useful.

WARNING: This is bleeding edge tech btw (caniuse), but figured it might be of use to someone

Sources:

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLCanvasElement/getContext#colortype
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/CanvasRenderingContext2D/getImageData#pixelformat

Q: A user access token is required to request this resource A:

A few lines after in the documentation it states

App access tokens can also be used to publish content to Facebook on behalf of a person who has granted a publishing permission to your application.

This is what they mean by requests on behalf of the user.

For the albums endpoint you need a user access token.

Yes your friends need to re-authenticate your app every two months if you extend a short lived user access token. The point is not to have apps sitting around with access when the user may have forgotten them. Prompting the user to re-authenticate ensures they are still aware of these apps and can have the choice to keep or delete them

Q: SMTPAddressFailedException: 550-Verification failed A:

What I suspect is that there is some configuration or policy which prevents the outgoing mails where the from address is not registered with it. If you problem is to configure an address where the users can reply to (and which should be different from the one you are authenticating), then there is a reply-to header which you can set.

Q: Microsoft Metadata Tags No Long Appear In Windows Explorer A:

Root Cause

Windows Explorer's Windows Property System (via the Media Foundation / Shell Property Handler) handles metadata differently depending on the container format and where the tags are stored:

  1. Microsoft:Category writes to XMP (XMP-microsoft:Category): In MP4/MOV containers, ExifTool stores this in an embedded XMP UUID atom (moov/trak/mdia/minf/stbl/stsd/... or top-level moov/udta/XMP_). Windows Explorer has notoriously inconsistent native support for reading non-standard XMP blocks from QuickTime/MP4 containers unless a third-party shell extension (like Icaros or old Windows Media Player codecs) was previously hooking into the property handler. Recent Windows 11 updates tightened sandboxing around Shell Property Handlers and default Media Foundation decoders, often bypassing raw embedded XMP for video files.

  2. Windows Explorer expects QuickTime User Data / Item List atoms: For .mp4 and .mov files, Windows Explorer natively maps the Details → Description → Tags field (canonical property System.Keywords) to native QuickTime metadata items, specifically:

    • QuickTime:Keywords / ItemList:Keywords (standard iTunes/QuickTime metadata atoms, e.g., ©key or keyw)

    • ItemList:Category (catg)

Solution: Write Native QuickTime / ItemList Metadata

Instead of targeting Microsoft:Category, write directly to the QuickTime item list metadata tags that Windows Shell natively maps to System.Keywords:

Bash

# Write tags/keywords to MP4/MOV
exiftool -ItemProperties:Keywords="tag1; tag2" -QuickTime:Keywords="tag1, tag2" <filename.mp4>

Or more generally across QuickTime tag slots:

Bash

exiftool -Keywords="tag1; tag2" -Category="tag1; tag2" <filename.mp4>

To ensure backward and cross-platform compatibility across Windows Explorer, Apple Photos, and Adobe tools, populate both native QuickTime atoms and XMP simultaneously:

Bash

exiftool -QuickTime:Keywords="tag1; tag2" -XMP-dc:Subject="tag1" -XMP-dc:Subject="tag2" -Microsoft:Category="tag1; tag2" <filename.mp4>

Inspecting Tags Added via File Properties

To see exactly where Windows Explorer writes tags when you set them through the GUI, run:

Bash

exiftool -G1 -a -s -v2 <filename.mp4> | findstr /i "tag keyword category"

(On PowerShell, use Select-String instead of findstr)

You will see that Windows writes directly to the moov.udta or moov.meta.ilst hierarchy rather than the XMP atom.

Q: How to call a statically linked Pascal function from a C main? A:

Full disclosure: I solemnly swear that I am not a robot. This answer has been solely generated by a natural intelligence tool.

[…] right now I'm struggling with Pascal.

You mean you are struggling with the Free Pascal Compiler, not Pascal in general. Pascal as a language does not define how to interface with different languages. Keep this in mind; you are tailoring your program to one Pascal implementation.

[…] I'm not forced to use fpc, please let me know if there's another decent compiler which would ease the process. […]

Well, development has stalled like over 16 years ago (hence you do not want to use it for any new projects), yet as a frontend to (an old version of) the GCC the GNU Pascal Compiler easily mediates between the languages:

  1. Amend your UCSD Pascal unit to use the GCC‐style attribute syntax and drop the Delphi C type calling convention cdecl modifier: 
    --- hello.pas~  2026-08-13 14:14:31.000000000 +0000
+++ hello.pas   2026-08-22 04:00:00.000000000 +0000
@@ -2,11 +2,11 @@

 interface

-procedure hello; cdecl; public name 'hello';
+procedure hello; attribute (name = 'hello');

 implementation

-procedure hello; cdecl;
+procedure hello;
 begin
     writeln('hello');
 end;
    The name attribute is a GPC extension.
  2. Call the GPC Run Time System initialization and finalization routines from your C code: 
    --- main.c~     2026-08-13 14:14:31.000000000 +0000
+++ main.c      2026-08-22 04:00:00.000000000 +0000
@@ -1,5 +1,7 @@
 void hello(void);

-int main(void) {
+int main(int argc, char **argv, char **envp) {
+    _p_initialize(argc, argv, envp, 0);
     hello();
+    _p_finalize();
 }
  3. Translate, compile, and link (uses ld of the GCC): 
    gpc -o hello hello.pas main.c
    NB: ldd still lists the dynamic dependencies of the C program (libc etc.).

Of course the GPC supports the other way round, importing foreign language stuff into a Pascal program.
